FINDINGS, RULINGS AND ORDER FOR ENTRY OF JUDGMENT : As a former
employee of the defendant, City of Lawrence, the plaintiff has
brought this action alleging three claims against the city, viz:
Count 1: Breach of contract for wages and benefits; Count 2: Quantum
Meruit and unjust enrichment, and; Court 3: Multiple Damages,
pursuant to G.L. Ch. 149, s. 150. The facts are not in dispute. Myles
E. Burke was employed by the City of Lawrence from 2001 to January 5,
2010, when his services as Commissioner of Inspectional Services were
terminated by the city's executive. Mr. Burke's status as an employee
with the city was co terminus . That is, as an appointee of the
city's executive, he was not covered under the provisions of G.L. Ch.
31 nor G.L. Ch. 150E. He thus had no civil service protection or
collective bargaining rights. In 1990, the Legislature enacted as one
of its special acts, chapter 41. The purpose of the statute was to
seek to bring the city's finances under control by way of outside
authority. Over the years, it has been alleged that the City of
Lawrence has experienced a history of fiscal ills resulting from over
spending, failure to maintain and improve its revenue basis,
mismanagement, self dealing, and cronyism . As part of the
Legislature's efforts to reign in this profound fiscal chaos, section
three of chapter 41 of the acts of 1990 was enacted and provides in
pertinent part "No personnel expenses earned or accrued within any
department, board, commission, agency or other unit of city
government shall be charged to or paid from any allotment of a
subsequent period without the written approval of the mayor, except
for subsequently determined retroactive compensation adjustments, or
in the case of an emergency involving the health or safety of the
people or their property". -two- Stripped of its legalese, what this
paragraph means is that all employees of the city from 1990 forward
must take their earned vacation and personal time as it accrues. They
cannot save or 'bank' it and then seek a lump sum payment (sometimes
referred to as a "golden handshake") when they retire or leave public
service. The purpose of the legislation is perfectly clear. It is to
balance and predict the city's financial obligations over the course
of each fiscal year, to control overspending and avoid the financial
shock associated with having to fund large lump sum payments to
employees when they leave the city's employ. It further permits the
city, not the employee, to control the line item costs of each
particular municipal position. This is so since the city can budget
for one, firm amount for a position and not face having to expend
more money because the employee elects to work through his/her
vacation, thereby requiring the city to appropriate more funds for
the position to pay for banked vacation time. In essence, as the
statute has been enacted by the Legislature, it becomes a management
rights reserved to the employer. During his years as a municipal
employee, the plaintiff served in various positions, most generally
in administrative posts and as a department head. As such he knew or
should have known of the implications of chapter 41 of the acts of
1990 since it directly affected the budgets of the department(s) he
headed. He was in fact one of the city's managers responsible for
carrying out the provisions of the statute. On June 23, 2010, the
city's executive terminated the plaintiff's services as Commissioner
of Inspectional Services with the City of Lawrence. The plaintiff
then claimed the amount of $58,003.80, representing unpaid accrued
vacation time, sick leave and furlough time. In response to the
requested payments, the city paid over to the plaintiff the amount of
$32,712.20 and refused to pay the balance of the plaintiff's claim
($25,290.60), identifying that amount as representing banked vacation
time, something prohibited by the Legislature's 1990 emergency fiscal
act. Both sides have briefed the issues and have now been heard
before the Court upon cross motions for summary judgment (Mass. R.
Civ. P. 56). Summary judgment is appropriate where there are no
genuine issues of material fact to be presented to a fact finder for
determination at trial (See: Augat v. Liberty Mutual Ins. Co., 410
Mass. 117, 1991. See also: Kourouvacilis v. General Motors Corp., 410
Mass. 706, 1991 and Celotex Corp. V. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 1986). In
the instant case, it is clear that by enacting ch 41 of the Acts of
1990, Legislature has moved to prohibit the banking of vacation and
other accrued time by employees of the City of Lawrence as a means of
bringing fiscal stability to the city's treasury. As a municipal
corporation under its -three- direct control and as a political
subdivision of the Commonwealth, with reference to the city and its
finances, the Legislature obviously has the authority to so act.
Since the passage of the 1990 statute has the force of law, there are
no genuine issues of material fact to be presented to a fact finder
at trial in determining the rights and responsibilities of the
parties in this matter. The plaintiff raises a series of issues in
seeking to prevail in his claims in this matter. He suggests that his
pay stubs from the city's payroll account have reflected accrued
vacation time and that as such he relied upon the same and is
entitled to relief. He also suggests that over the years the city has
seen fit to pay banked vacation time to others upon their separation
from city service. He points to the fact that he was not given
adequate notice of the legislative enactment and that it is illegal,
illogical and unfair to be denied his claims by the city. He further
points to the provisions of G.L. Ch. 149 as amended (the so called
Massachusetts "wage act") amended to include certain public employees
after the enactment of Ch. 41 of the Acts of 1990 as further grounds
for relief. Each of these circumstances and justifications cannot
overcome the Legislature's black letter law enactment which prohibits
the banking of accrued time as a means of bringing fiscal control to
the city. In enacting the 1990 special act the Legislature did not
violate its own enactment of G.L. Ch. 149. The Legislature did not
direct the city not to pay vacation time to its employees. It did say
paid vacation time must be taken when it is earned. It cannot be
banked to be later "cashed in" as a lump sum payment and further
expense to a cash strapped city. That is the essence of the
Legislature's legitimate exercise of its authority in this case.
Pronounced in the vernacular, city employees must "take it or lose
it" when it comes to earned vacation time. The suggestion that other
former employees have had the benefit of banked vacation time after
1990 again affords the plaintiff no relief. If the city has violated
the statute in the past, then the law dictates how such violations
are to be remedied. Otherwise, the violations do not form a basis for
others (including the plaintiff) to receive any benefit. Finally, the
plaintiff's claim that he was not put on notice of the statute by his
employer is simply untenable. All persons are presumed to be on
notice of the law as enacted by the Commonwealth's Legislature and
signed by its Governor. In this case, as a department head charged
with the responsibility to carry out the law for the benefit of the
municipality he was employed to serve, the argument truly becomes
absurd. ORDER FOR ENTRY OF JUDGMENT : Upon cross motions brought
seeking summary judgment in this matter and after hearing, review of
the parties' submissions and upon a Rule 56 standard, the plaintiff's
motion for summary judgment in this matter is DENIED. The defendant
City of Lawrence's motion seeking summary judgment is ALLOWED. There
being no issue of material fact to present to a finder of fact after
-four- trial, based upon the Legislature's 1990 statutory enactment,
said defendant is now entitled to judgment in this case as a matter
of law. Judgment of dismissal, with prejudice shall now be entered
upon the docket for the defendant City of Lawrence in this matter and
there shall be no award of attorneys' fees or costs at this time.
Notice shall be provided to the parties pursuant to Rule 58. By the
Court: Hon. Robert A. Cornetta, Justice May 31, 2012 : (Robert A.
Cornetta, Justice)

74385071.description: Defendant's motion to dismiss-While the grand jury minutes on page 9 indicate that Inv. Kirchner used the feminine pronoun "her" when referring to the person who entered the house to retrieve the gun, it seems readily apparent that he either misspoke or t hat there is an error in the transcription of the minutes. I reach that conclusion because subsequent questioning by both the prosecutor and the grand jurors made it clear that no one believed or suggested that the defendant ever had the gun in her hand. If Inv. Kirchner did misspeak, h is action was, at worse negligence, and did not constitute intentional or reckless conduct. Moreover, in light of the tenor of the subsequent questioning, I do not believe that his misstatement made a difference in the grand jury's decision to indict. See Commonwealth v. Mayfield, 398 Mass. 615, 621-622 (1986). With respect to the testimony given on pages 14 and 15 of the grand jury minutes, it is true that Krupa did not expressly say in his written statement that the defendant was aware of the transaction. However, he said enough to warrant such an inference. A prosecutor is not required to present all exculpatory evidence to a grand jury, but she "must disclose evidence that would greatly undermine the credibility of evidence likely to affect the gran jury's decision to indict." Commonwealth v. Ali, 43 Mass.App.Ct. 549, 557 (1997). I do not believe that Krupa's written statement greatly undermined the credibility of the evidence presented, or that the failure to present that statement to the grand jury affected their decision to indict. I take a dim view of Inv. Kirchner's editorial comment on page 15: "Unless she's wearing earplugs or blindfolded." Police officers testifying before a grand jury should recite the facts, not offer their opinions (unless, of course, they are giving proper expert testimony). However, even though the imporper portion of the witness's answer would be inadmmissible at trial, it was generally responsive to a grand juror's question. See Commonwealth v. Freeman, 407 Mass. 279, 284 (1990). It therefore appears that the prosecutor and the witness did not undertake to present that opinion to the grand jury in order to procure an indictment. See Commonwealth v. Champagne, 399 Mass. 80, 84 (1987). Finally, having in mind that the standard at this stage is probable cause and not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, I conclude that the evidence presented to the grand jury, while thin, was sufficient to support the indictments. Accordingly, the motion is Denied (Ford, J.).
